Project: Armada / Concord Protocol
Severity: High
Status: Resolved & Patched

Vulnerability

A permission-validation flaw in Concord's control-plane event handling allowed any community member to strip another member's roles by sending an unauthorized role-revocation event (kind 3308). The delegation fixpoint only checked roles a signer granted, not roles they revoked — so an empty role_ids edition passed vacuously for any signer, regardless of their authority level.

Impact: Any member could break another member's channel access and permissions. Affected members lost admin roles, channel visibility, and required a ban/kick/reinvite cycle to partially restore access.

Disclosure & Resolution

• Reported: Jul 13, 2026
• Patched: Jul 13, 2026 — same day
• Fix: 5a655112 (https://gitlab.com/soapbox-pub/armada/-/commit/5a6551127fec11cbf69d27dc140010db72419683) — "Drop control-plane revokes and demotions from non-authority signers" by Chad Curtis
• Issue: soapbox-pub/armada#73 (https://gitlab.com/soapbox-pub/armada/-/work_items/73)

The patch enforces that a non-owner signer must hold MANAGE_ROLES, outrank everything handed out, and outrank what the admissible predecessor conferred — closing both the vacuous-revoke and rank-bypass paths.

$1,000 USD awarded to hzrd149 for responsible disclosure of a high-severity authorization bypass.

ECAI extends that logic from isolated proofs to globally connected structure.

A ZKP answers:

“Can this claim be proven without revealing its witness?”

ECAI asks the larger question:

“Where does this verified claim belong in the global structure of knowledge?”

A conventional proof is usually local: one statement, one computation, one verifier.

ECAI treats verification as compositional. Each verified relationship can become part of a wider, traversable proof structure—independently reproduced, recombined and checked across distributed nodes.

ZKP protects the hidden witness.

ECAI aims to preserve the relationships around it.

The distinction is:

ZKP proves that a result is valid.
ECAI proves how the result connects.

Not merely proof of knowledge, but proof of structure.

Not isolated certainty, but a global verification fabric.

Not intelligence generated behind a closed model, but intelligence assembled from relationships that can be tested.

When proof becomes reusable structure, verification stops being the final step of computation.

It becomes the substrate of intelligence.

Proof of Work scales because it is enforced by mathematics.

Proof of Law does not scale because it depends on unequal enforcement.

Bitcoin changes the enforcement model. Hash power doesn't care about status. Consensus doesn't negotiate. Verification is applied uniformly to every participant.

Hi, Nostrich

With a help from claude, I’m working on a fun little OSS project called "wired".  🔥

https://github.com/Hakkadaikon/wired/blob/main/docs/arch/overview.md

It’s a high-performance SDK written purely in C - with absolutely zero dependency on libc.

It includes a full protocol stack for TLS 1.3, QUIC, HTTP/3, and WebTransport. 
Under the hood, it features built-in CPU core pinning and a polling driver powered by 
- eBPF (an in-kernel VM) 
- XDP (a high-speed packet processing framework)

The craziest part? The whole thing runs as a single binary of just about 200KB.

Right now, I'm deep into testing and debugging. I've finally managed to get a basic WebTransport connection working with a simple example, though there are still plenty of bugs to squash.

I've been developing it on a VPS, but since testing XDP in a virtual environment has its limits, I'll probably end up buying a physical bare-metal machine for proper testing soon.

This project is the culmination of everything I’ve wanted to build over the last 2-3 years. Looking ahead,
